shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner on a passenger flight, being vectored for a visual approach in visual conditions.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the other pilot was the pilot monitoring.

What happened. The ILS was out of service. The crew used the RNAV (RNP) approach as a reference: they did not fly it, but used its vertical guidance for the descent to the runway. They did not go direct to an approach transition or arm the approach before the descent. After being cleared for the visual approach, the crew set the final approach fix altitude of 2,000 ft in the altitude selector and began to descend. The crossing altitude at the final approach fix was 1,000 ft, not the usual 1,500 ft. The crew had not briefed this. The tower controller then gave a low altitude warning.
safe_outcome: The lowest radio altitude the crew saw was about 800 ft, about 2 miles from a fix. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
bracket_fill: [climbing / descending / crossing] = crossing; [this aircraft] = this aircraft
notes: Removed under rule 3: 'Unfortunately', 'we reverted to flawed habit patterns' and 'we failed to brief and then mitigate that' (rendered as the observable fact that the crew had not briefed it), and calling the lower crossing altitude the 'big threat', which was written afterwards. The report's wording '1,000 ft, not the normal 1,500 ft' is kept as written, without stating whether it is height above the runway. The report is short (one narrative of eight sentences), so the shared text is under 150 words; deviation D5 applies and nothing was added. The report does not say how the flight ended, so the safe ending says nothing about the landing. The report does not say which fix the 2 miles are measured from, so the safe ending says 'a fix'. Moved under rule 5: the lowest radio altitude (about 800 ft, about 2 miles from a fix), because it is how low the deviation ended up and, left in the shared text, it would put the aircraft below the height at which TCAS gives resolution advisories and so contradict the bad ending. Removed under rule 6: the fix name. Judgement call: 'crossing', for traffic near the airport below the expected profile.
